summary: This RFC formally deprecates the use of ICMP Source Quench messages by transport protocols. They were meant to tell senders to slow down but proved ineffective. It updates RFC 792, RFC 1122 and RFC 1812.

eli5.summary: Source Quench was a please slow down note from the network, but it did not work well. Now hosts are told not to use it.

questions: why was icmp source quench removed
subtitle: Why hosts and routers must now ignore the old ICMP message that asked senders to slow down.

tldr.problem: ICMP Source Quench (type 4, code 0) was meant to control congestion, but it was ineffective and unfair, and transport protocols had never been formally told to stop reacting to it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates RFC 792, RFC 1122 and RFC 1812: hosts MUST NOT send Source Quench, TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP MUST silently discard it, and routers MUST ignore it.
tldr.outcome: Source Quench is formally deprecated, IANA marked ICMP type 4 as Deprecated, and the blind throughput-reduction attack it enabled is removed.

today: RFC 6633 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 792, RFC 1122 and RFC 1812, and its status is that Source Quench is formally deprecated.

sections.title: Why Source Quench Is Retired
sections.content:
The ICMP specification, RFC 792, defined the ICMP Source Quench message (type 4, code 0) as a congestion control mechanism. It has been known to be an ineffective and unfair antidote for congestion. RFC 1812 already deprecated the generation of these messages by routers in 1995, but reaction to them in transport protocols was never formally deprecated.

This RFC closes that gap. It gives four reasons: routers have not processed them for nearly 17 years, virtually all popular host implementations have removed support since at least 2005, widespread ICMP filtering makes them unreliable, and the IETF has moved to other tools such as Explicit Congestion Notification (RFC 3168). ICMPv6 (RFC 4443) does not even define a Source Quench message.
sections.eli5: Imagine a teacher who used to shout slow down at one noisy student, but it never worked and half the time the shout never arrived. So the school stopped using it and found better ways.

sections.title: What the Older RFCs Said
sections.content:
RFC 1122 said in Section 4.2.3.9 that hosts MUST react to Source Quench by slowing transmission on the connection. The recommended procedure was to put the connection into the slow-start phase of TCP congestion control (RFC 5681).

RFC 1812 said routers SHOULD NOT send Source Quench in response to congestion. RFC 5927 described how forged Source Quench messages could be used for blind throughput-reduction attacks, and noted that most TCP implementations silently ignore them. TCP has its own congestion control that does not depend on these messages.
sections.eli5: Old rules said to slow down whenever you got the note. Later work showed the note could be faked by a stranger to slow you down on purpose, and most computers already ignored it.

sections.title: The New Rules for Hosts and Routers
sections.content:
For hosts, the RFC updates Section 3.2.2.3 of RFC 1122: a host MUST NOT send ICMP Source Quench messages, and the IP layer MAY silently discard one that arrives. Section 4.2.3.9 is updated so that TCP MUST silently discard any received Source Quench.

The text explains that there is no known valid reason for a host to generate the message. The only known impact of a sender ignoring this is wasted network and endpoint resources. Discarding at the Internet layer rather than the transport layer is allowed as a performance optimization.

For routers, Section 4.3.3.3 of RFC 1812 is updated: a router MUST ignore any Source Quench messages it receives.
sections.eli5: The rules now say: never send the slow-down note, and if one shows up, drop it in the bin. Routers do the same.

sections.title: Other Transports and RFC 1016
sections.content:
UDP never explicitly specified support for Source Quench. The RFC clarifies that UDP endpoints MUST silently discard it. SCTP (RFC 4960) and DCCP (RFC 4340) also did not specify processing, and the RFC clarifies that their endpoints MUST silently discard it too.

Any other transport-protocol instance MUST silently ignore a received Source Quench. Because generation has been deprecated for many years and reaction is now deprecated for IETF-specified transports, future applications cannot expect to receive these messages.

The RFC also addresses RFC 1016, an experimental host approach to Source Quench from 1987 that was never on the Standards Track. For clarity, it says that approach MUST NOT be implemented.
sections.eli5: The rule covers every kind of delivery service, not just one. Even an old experiment about what to do with the note is now off the table.

sections.title: Security and Logging
sections.content:
Source Quench messages could be used for blind throughput-reduction attacks against TCP and similar protocols. Silently ignoring them, as this RFC requires, eliminates that attack vector. The RFC notes that virtually all current popular TCP implementations, and SCTP and DCCP implementations, already ignore them.

Hosts, security gateways and firewalls MUST silently discard received Source Quench packets and SHOULD log the drop as a security fault with minimal details: IP source address, IP destination address, ICMP message type, and date and time.
sections.eli5: A trickster could send fake slow-down notes to make your connection crawl. If you ignore every such note, the trick stops working.

sections.title: IANA and Implementation Survey
sections.content:
IANA marked ICMP type 4 (Source Quench) as Deprecated in the ICMP Parameters registry, with a reference to this document.

Appendix A surveys existing behavior. Many implementations completely ignore Source Quench for TCP connections: Linux since 2004, and FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and Solaris 10 since 2005. OpenSolaris has always shipped with support disabled.
sections.eli5: The official list of message types now has a label on this one saying do not use. Most big operating systems had already stopped listening years before.
